## Hearty Greetings <note>original: "S. P." for Salutem Plurimam, a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

This is the time when the most renowned Master* **JOSEPH PITTON TOURNEFORT** <note>Tournefort (1656–1708) was a pioneering French botanist whose system of classification was widely used before Linnaeus.</note>, *the most diligent student of plants and of the whole*

# PREFACE

*Natural History is, as it were, a most richly stocked storehouse. For three years (namely 1686, 87, and 88) which I spent in Paris, I diligently attended the botanical lectures of this most learned man <note>Likely referring to Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, who began teaching at the Jardin des Plantes in 1683</note>. I excerpted and recorded from his own lips the names of all the plants in the same order in which they were arranged in the Garden, and as they were pointed out by that praised man—truly a delightful spectacle and the greatest pleasure for all lovers of botany <term>Botanophilorum: literally "friends of plants," referring to early modern botanical enthusiasts</term>.*

*The other source is the Index and, as it were, the Introduction <term>Prodromus: a preliminary publication intended to precede a fuller work</term> to the "Batavian Paradise" <note>Referring to the "Paradisus Batavus," a catalog of the plants in the Leyden Botanical Garden</note>, drawn up by Mr. Paul Hermann, public Professor of Medicine and Botany at the University of Leiden <note>original: "Academia Lugduno Batava"</note>. He was a man most skilled in the knowledge of all natural things, and especially of exotic species, in which are presented more than—*

# PREFACE

*Once I had obtained these from the gardeners <note>original: "ab Hortulanis"; referring to the professional keepers of botanical gardens</note>, nothing was of greater concern to me than that my collected plants should be marked with their proper names. For this reason, I formed a plan to bring my collection of plants to the praised Hermann <note>Paul Hermann (1646–1695), a celebrated German physician and botanist who served as the Director of the Leiden Botanical Garden</note> and to ask that he might deign to teach me their legitimate names.*

*This plan turned out so successfully for me that this most refined man, noticing my great passion for the philosophy of plants <note>original: "phytoſophiam"; the study of the nature and classification of plants</note>, most generously promised me his assistance. Furthermore—which I had not expected—he immediately and of his own accord offered me all of his own writings to read and transcribe. These were the works he had composed concerning the rarer stems <note>original: "ſtirpibus"; often used to mean plant species or stocks</note> observed by him in the Gardens of the Dutch <note>original: "Hortis Batavorum"</note> under the title of the **Dutch Paradise** <note>original: "Paradiſi Batavi", Hermann's famous posthumous work published in 1698</note>. On that same occasion, it also happened that each individual plant,*

<summary>The author describes seeking the expertise of the botanist Paul Hermann to correctly identify his plant collection, resulting in Hermann granting him access to his unpublished manuscripts on rare Dutch garden plants.</summary>
<keywords>Paul Hermann, botanical nomenclature, Paradise Batavus, Dutch gardens, plant collecting, phytosophy</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's account of his collaboration with Paul Hermann, describing the inspiration for his botanical index and the encouragement he received from the scientific community. Continuity from previous page: "...each individual plant,"</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

*which had been described in the **Dutch Paradise** <note>original: "Paradiso Batavo"</note>, dried from life <note>original: "ad vivum siccatæ"; a method of preserving plants so they retain their natural appearance</note> with extraordinary brilliance and fixed to paper sheets, were shown to me. I must publicly confess that I have never seen anything more elegant than this work. Because of this, it happened that I excerpted all their naming systems <note>original: "nomenclaturas"</note> in that same order in which they were arranged in the **Paradise**, and distinguished them with the title of **Index** or **Prodromus** <note>original: "Prodromi"; a Latin term for a preliminary work or "forerunner" intended to precede a more comprehensive volume</note>.*

*Furthermore, as to why I have brought both of these Indices to public light, I did so at the requests and urgings of the most esteemed leaders of the botanical arts <note>original: "Rei Herbariæ Procerum"</note>, who judged that the studies of plant-lovers <note>original: "Botanophilorum"</note> would be excellently promoted by it, and that no small advantage would reach the public good.*

*Enjoy these things, therefore, Kind Reader <note>original: "Benevole Lector"</note>, until the Catalog of the Royal*

Greater scented purple **TOADFLAX** with narrower leaves, **Caspar Bauhin**. <note>original: "Linaria purpurea major odorata foliis angustioribus C. B." The genus name *Linaria* comes from *Linum* (flax), as their leaves often resemble those of the flax plant.</note>

Evergreen **TOADFLAX**, **Prospero Alpini**'s *On Exotic Plants*. <note>original: "Linaria sempervirens Prosp. Alp. de Exot." Prospero Alpini was a Venetian physician and botanist who famously described flora from Egypt and the Mediterranean.</note>

First Pannonian **TOADFLAX**, **Carolus Clusius**. <note>original: "Linaria Pannonica 1 Clus." Clusius was a foundational figure in modern botany; Pannonia refers to a region in Central Europe encompassing parts of modern-day Hungary and Austria.</note>

Annual narrow-leaved **TOADFLAX** with small white flowers and longer spurs, **Giovanni Battista Triumfetti**. <note>original: "Linaria annua angustifolia flosculis albis longius caudatis Triumph." In botany, 'caudatis' (tailed) refers to the long nectar spurs at the back of the flower.</note>

Scented Montpellier **TOADFLAX**, **Johann Bauhin**. <note>original: "Linaria odorata Monspessulana I. B." Montpellier was a major center for botanical study in France during the Renaissance.</note>

**TOADFLAX** with Bedstraw-like leaves, **Paolo Boccone**. <note>original: "Linaria Molluginis folio Bocc." Paolo Boccone was a Sicilian botanist and Cistercian monk known for his detailed illustrations.</note>

Mountain yellow **TOADFLAX** with leaves like Dyer's Greenweed, **Caspar Bauhin**. <note>original: "Linaria lutea montana Genistæ tinctoriæ folio C. B." Dyer's Greenweed (*Genista tinctoria*) was a shrub widely used to produce yellow dye.</note>

*Dwarf Alpine **TOADFLAX** with sea-green leaves and a golden throat.* <note>original: "Linaria Alpina pumila glauco folio rictu aureo." 'Glaucous' (glauco) describes the waxy, blue-grey or sea-green coating found on many alpine plants.</note>

**Pointed-leaved curly dock**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Sharp curly dock**, **Tabernaemontanus.** <note>original: "Lapathum acutum crispum." Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus was a 16th-century herbalist famous for his detailed woodcut illustrations.</note>
**Wavy Parisian dock**, **Royal Garden of Paris.** **Beautiful wavy Bolognese dock**, **Johann Bauhin.** **Violin dock.** <note>original: "Lapathum violon." This refers to *Rumex pulcher*, named "violin dock" because the shape of the leaf resembles the body of a violin.</note>
**Roundish-leaved dock**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Common blunt-leaved dock**, **Johann Bauhin.**
**Round-leaved Alpine dock**, **Johann Bauhin.** **Round-leaved mountain Horse-dock**, **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "Hippolapathum." From the Greek *hippos* (horse), a prefix used in botany to signify a large or coarse version of a plant.</note>
**Most excellent dock, called the Apothecary’s Rhubarb**, **Morison.** **Rhubarb.** <note>original: "Lapathum præstantissimum Rhabarbarum officinarum dictum" and "Rheubarbe." Robert Morison was a Scottish botanist and the first Professor of Botany at Oxford. This entry refers to medicinal rhubarb, highly valued for its laxative properties.</note>
**Oily dock with a triangular leaf**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Good King Henry**, **Johann Bauhin.** <note>original: "Bonus Henricus." Now known as *Blitum bonus-henricus*, this plant was a common perennial vegetable, often cooked like spinach.</note>
**Stinking sea dock**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Wavy sea dock**, **Johann Bauhin.**
**Greatest mountain SORREL**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Greatest wild sorrel**, **Johann Bauhin.** <note>original: "ACETOSA." Sorrels are related to docks but are distinguished by their acidic, pleasant taste, often used in soups and salads.</note>
**Greatest mountain sorrel with curly leaves**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Curly sorrel**, **Johann Bauhin.** <note>original: "Oxalis crispa." *Oxalis* is another name used historically for sour plants containing oxalic acid.</note>

# The Royal Garden of Paris

**Blood-red beet with a large, turnip-like root**, **Royal Garden of Paris.** **Large red beet**, **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "Beta sanguinea magnâ radice Rapæ" and "Beta rubra major." Caspar Bauhin (C.B.) was a Swiss botanist who categorized thousands of plants, a precursor to modern taxonomy.</note>
**Beet with flame-colored leaves and stems**, **Royal Garden of Paris.** <note>original: "Beta foliis & caule flammeis." This likely refers to a variety of Swiss chard or a colorful beetroot variant.</note>
**Golden-ribbed beet with a large, turnip-like root**, **Royal Garden of Paris.**
**Large yellow beet**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Beet with a boxwood-colored root**, **Cesalpino.** <note>original: "Beta major lutea" and "Beta radice Buxeâ." Andrea Cesalpino (Cesalp.) was an Italian physician and botanist who classified plants based on their fruits and seeds.</note>
**Wild sea beet**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Spontaneous wild sea beet**, **Lobelius.** <note>original: "Beta sylvestris maritima" and "Beta sylvestris spontanea marina." Matthias de l'Obel (Lobelius) was a Flemish botanist; the flower Lobelia is named after him. Sea beet is the wild ancestor of modern beets and chard.</note>
**Cretan beet with prickly seeds**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Cretan beet with thorny seeds**, **Johann Bauhin.** <note>original: "Beta Cretica semine aculeato/spinoso." Johann Bauhin (I.B.) was the brother of Caspar; the two often collaborated but published separate seminal works.</note>

**White or pale-green garden orache**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **Orache, "good women’s leaves."** <note>original: "Atriplex hortensis alba, sive pallide virens" and the French "Arroche, follettes bonnes-dames." Orache, also known as "mountain spinach," was a common potherb.</note>
**Red garden orache**, **Caspar Bauhin and Johann Bauhin.**
**Another cultivated orache with purple-tinted leaves and flowers**, **Lobelius.** <note>original: "Atriplex sativa altera folio & flore purpureo livens."</note>

**Wild orache with spear-shaped or triangular leaves**, **Catalog of the Royal Garden of Blois.** <note>original: "Atriplex sylvestris folio hastato sive deltoide." The "Hortus Regius Blesensis" (Hort. Reg. Bles.) was the garden of Gaston, Duke of Orléans.</note>
**Broad-leaved wild orache**, **Caspar Bauhin.** **The orache called "Goosefoot"**, **Johann Bauhin.** <note>original: "Atriplex sylvestris latifolia" and "Pes Anserinus." Greater **HELIOTROPE** of Dioscorides, **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "HELIOTROPIUM majus Diofcoridis." # CHICKWEED <note>original: "ALSINE." This genus includes plants commonly known today as Chickweeds and Stitchworts.</note>

Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) was a Swiss botanist who famously categorized thousands of plants, bridging the gap between ancient herbalism and modern botany.</note> **Warty Chicory or Zacintha, to be numbered among the Hawkweeds**, according to **Jean Bauhin.** <note>original: "Cichorium verrucosum sive Zacintha Hieraciis annumerandum." Jean Bauhin was Caspar’s brother; the two often had slightly different classifications for the same species.</note>

**A certain jagged-leaved relative of Chondrilla, perhaps the Trinciatella**, according to **Jean Bauhin.** <note>original: "Chondrillis affinis laciniata quædam an Trinciatella."</note> **Smooth, narrow-leaved Sow-thistle**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "Sonchus lævis angustifolius." Sonchus is the genus of sow-thistles, known for their milky sap and yellow flowers.</note>

**Marsh tree-like Hawkweed**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "Hieracium arborescens palustre." Hieracium, or Hawkweed, was named from the Greek "hierax" (hawk), based on an ancient belief that hawks ate the plant to sharpen their eyesight.</note> **Tree-like Sow-thistle**, according to **Tabernaemontanus.** <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1522–1590) was an early German botanist and physician.</note>

**Greater Hawkweed with a Sow-thistle leaf, or Sow-thistle Hawkweed**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** **Creeping Sow-thistle, called by many the Greater Hawkweed**, according to **Jean Bauhin.** <note>original: "Sonchus repens multis Hieracium majus."</note>

**Greater Hawkweed with a Sow-thistle leaf and a curved seed**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** **Prickly, jagged Cretan Sow-thistle**, by the **same author.** <note>original: "Sonchus asper laciniatus Creticus Ejusd." "Ejusd." (Ejusdem) refers back to the previously mentioned author, Caspar Bauhin.</note>

**Yellow Viper’s-bugloss-like Hawkweed with heads like a Blessed Thistle**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** <note>original: "Hieracium Echioides luteum capitulis Cardui benedicti." "Echioides" implies a resemblance to Echium (Viper's-bugloss). The Blessed Thistle (Carduus benedictus) was a well-known medicinal plant.</note> **Very large Hawkweed with Blessed Thistle heads, called Viper’s-bugloss Bugloss by some**, according to **Jean Bauhin.**

**Mountain Hawkweed with long, slender stems**, according to **Columna.** <note>original: "Hieracium montanum leptomacrocaulon." Fabio Columna (1567–1640) was an Italian botanist. "Leptomacrocaulon" is a Greek-derived descriptor: 'leptos' (slender), 'macros' (long), and 'caulos' (stem).</note>

**Smooth, broad-leaved shrubby Hawkweed with toothed leaves**, according to **Caspar Bauhin.** **The second type of Greater broad-leaved Hawkweed**, or according to **Clusius.** <note>original: "Hieracium majus latifolium vel II. Clus." Carolus Clusius (1526–1609) was one of the most influential botanists of the 16th century, responsible for introducing the tulip to Europe.</note>

**WHITE FIR OR FEMALE FIR** <note>original: "Abies alba sive fœmina"</note> **of C. Bauhin.** <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a Swiss botanist whose "Pinax" (1623) standardized plant names. This is the European Silver Fir (*Abies alba*).</note> **Female fir or *elate thēleia*** <note>Greek: ἐλάτη θήλεια</note> **of J. Bauhin.** <note>Johann Bauhin (1541–1613), Caspar’s brother and author of a massive universal history of plants.</note>

**RED FIR OR THE FIRST GREAT SPRUCE** <note>original: "Abies rubra sive Picea major prima"</note> **of C. Bauhin.** <note>The Norway Spruce (*Picea abies*).</note> **The Spruce of the Romans, or *elate arrhēn*** <note>Greek: ἐλάτη ἄῤῥεν, meaning "male fir"</note> **and the Male Fir of Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany." Ancient authors often categorized similar plants as "male" and "female" based on perceived vigor or fruit-bearing habits.</note> **according to J. Bauhin.**

**LARCH** <note>original: "LARIX"</note> **of C. Bauhin. Cone-bearing larch with deciduous leaves** <note>original: "Larix folio deciduo conifera"</note> **of J. Bauhin.** <note>The European Larch (*Larix decidua*), notable among conifers for shedding its needles in autumn.</note>

**NON-STINKING GREATER OR ALPINE BEAN-TREFOIL** <note>original: "Anagyris non fœtida major vel Alpina"</note> **of C. Bauhin. The three-leaved Laburnum tree, similar to the bean-trefoil, of J. Bauhin.** <note>The Alpine Laburnum or Golden Chain Tree (*Laburnum alpinum*), which resembles the *Anagyris* but lacks the scent.</note>

**NON-STINKING BROAD-LEAFED BEAN-TREFOIL with flowers more densely clustered in a shorter bunch.** <note>original: "Anagyris non fœtida latifolia floribus densius congestis in breviorem uvam."</note>

**ACACIA WITH SCORPION-LIKE LEGUME LEAVES** <note>original: "Acacia foliis Scorpioidis leguminosæ"</note> **of C. Bauhin. True Acacia of J. Bauhin.** <note>Likely the Gum Arabic tree (*Acacia nilotica*), whose pods were compared by ancient botanists to the shape of a scorpion.</note>

**ETHIOPIAN BLADDER-SENNA WITH SCARLET FLOWERS** <note>original: "Colutea Æthiopica flore phœniceo." *Colutea* is a genus of shrubs in the pea family, famous for their inflated, air-filled seed pods that pop when squeezed.</note>
**JUPITER’S BEARD WITH THE SAME LEAVES** <note>original: "Barba Jovis foliis Ejusdem." *Barba Jovis* (Jupiter's Beard) generally refers to *Anthyllis barba-jovis*, a shrub with silvery, silky foliage.</note> **from the *Prodromus*.** <note>The *Prodromus* (1620) was a landmark work by the Swiss botanist Caspar Bauhin that served as a precursor to his great botanical index.</note>
**SILVER CEYLON BLADDER-SENNA, ENTIRELY SILVERY** <note>original: "Colutea Zeilanica argentea tota."</note> **from the *Garden of Leiden*.** <note>The *Hortus Lugduno-Batavus* is the famous botanical garden of Leiden University in the Netherlands, one of the oldest in the world.</note>
**GREATER SCORPION-PODDED OR SILIQUOSE BLADDER-SENNA** <note>original: "Colutea Scorpioides sive siliquosa major." *Scorpioides* describes seed pods that curve or twist like a scorpion's tail.</note> **according to Caspar Bauhin.** **SCORPION-PODDED BLADDER-SENNA according to Johann Bauhin.** <note>The brothers Caspar and Johann Bauhin were the preeminent botanical authorities of this era; their works attempted to clear up the confusion of plant names.</note>
**MARITIME SCORPION-PODDED BLADDER-SENNA WITH SEA-GREEN LEAVES** <note>original: "Colutea Scorpioides maritima glauco folio." *Glauco* refers to a pale blue or greyish-green waxy coating common on coastal plants.</note> **according to Caspar Bauhin.**

**ITALIAN SENNA, OR SENNA WITH BLUNT LEAVES** <note>original: "Senna Italica sive foliis obtusis." *Senna* species have been used since antiquity as medicinal purgatives.</note> **according to Caspar Bauhin.**
**FLORENTINE SENNA WITH LEAVES ALMOST HEART-SHAPED AT THE TIP** <note>original: "Senna Florentina foliis per extremum pene cordatis."</note> **according to Johann Bauhin.**
**WESTERN SENNA WITH A POISONOUS OPIUM SCENT, AND SMOOTH POINTED LEAVES LIKE THE PANNONIAN BITTER-VETCH** <note>original: "Senna Occidentalis odore Opii viroso, Orobi Pannonici foliis mucronatis glabra." *Viroso* implies a strong, unpleasant, or toxic smell.</note> **from the *Garden of Leiden*.**
**SMALLER WESTERN SENNA WITH A POISONOUS OPIUM SCENT AND SMOOTH BLUNT LEAVES** <note>original: "Senna Occidentalis odore Opii viroso, minus foliis glabris obtusis."</note> **from the *Garden of Leiden*.**

**BEAUTIFULLY SHINING JUPITER’S BEARD** <note>original: "Barba Jovis pulchre lucens."</note> **according to Johann Bauhin.**
**JUPITER’S BEARD** <note>original: "Barba Jovis."</note> **according to Camerarius.** <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598) was a German physician and botanist known for his detailed plant illustrations.</note>

**THE WINE-BEARING GRAPEVINE** <note>original: "Vitis vinifera."</note> **according to Caspar and Johann Bauhin.**
**COLUMELLA’S EARLY-RIPENING GRAPEVINE** <note>original: "Vitis præcox Columellæ." Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella was a Roman citizen who wrote extensively on agriculture and viticulture in the 1st century AD.</note> **from the *Royal Garden of Paris*.**
**GRAPEVINE WITH JAGGED LEAVES** <note>original: "Vitis laciniatis foliis."</note> **according to Cordus.** <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544) was a German botanist who authored one of the first modern pharmacopoeias and explored the flora of Central Europe.</note> **CELERY-LEAVED GRAPEVINE** <note>original: "Vitis Apii folio."</note> **according to Johann Bauhin.**

# The Royal Garden of Paris

**COMMON WHITE-FLOWERED JASMINE** <note>original: "JASMINUM vulgatius flore albo." Recorded by Caspar Bauhin (C. B.). Jasmine has been prized since antiquity for its intense fragrance.</note>
**Jasmine or Gelseminum with white flowers** <note>original: "Jasminum sive Gelseminum flore albo." Citations to I. B. refer to the work of Johann Bauhin.</note>
**Lower jasmine with large flowers** <note>original: "Jasminum humilius magno flore." A dwarf variety noted for its disproportionately large blooms.</note>
**Spanish jasmine with larger flowers, reddish on the outside** <note>original: "Jasminum Hispanicum flore majore externe rubente." This likely refers to *Jasminum grandiflorum*, known for its pink-tinged buds.</note>
**The same with double flowers.** <note>original: "*Idem flore duplici." "Double" flowers are mutations where the reproductive parts (stamens) become petals, creating a fuller bloom.</note>
**Yellow Jasmine or Gelseminum.** **Lower yellow jasmine.** <note>original: "Jasminum sive Gelseminum luteum" and "Jasminum humilius luteum."</note>
**Fragrant yellow jasmine** from the *Royal Garden of Paris*. <note>original: "Jasminum flavum odoratum."</note> **Highly fragrant yellow Indian Gelseminum.** <note>original: "Gelseminum Indicum flavum odoratissimum."</note>
**Yellow jasmine commonly called berry-bearing.** <note>original: "Jasminum luteum vulgo dictum bacciferum." Unlike many other jasmines, this variety produced noticeable fruit.</note> **Shrubby Trefoil, called by some yellow-flowered Polemonium.** <note>original: "Trifolium fruticans quibusdam Polemonium flore luteo." At this time, botanical naming was often inconsistent, leading to various names for the same plant.</note>
**Greatest jasmine with odorless scarlet flowers** from the *Royal Garden of Paris*. <note>original: "Jasminum maximum flore phoeniceo inodoro." *Phoeniceo* indicates a brilliant scarlet or crimson color.</note> **Indian Gelseminum with scarlet flowers.** <note>original: "Gelseminum Indicum flore phoeniceo."</note>
**Jasmine with Milfoil leaves.** <note>original: "Jasminum Millefolii folio." *Millefolii* refers to leaves that are finely divided, similar to Yarrow.</note> **Quamoclit.** <note>original: "Quamoclit." Known today as the Cypress Vine or Hummingbird Vine.</note>

**BLUE SYRINGA.** <note>original: "SYRINGA coerulea." In early modern botany, *Syringa* was a broad term that eventually became the scientific name for Lilacs, though it was once also used for Mock-oranges (*Philadelphus*).</note> **Syringa with blue flowers, or Lilac.** <note>original: "Syringa flore coeruleo sive Lilac."</note>
**Syringa or Lilac with deep purple flowers** from the *Edinburgh Garden*. <note>original: "Syringa sive Lilac flore saturate purpureo." *Hort. Edinburg.* refers to the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, established as a physic garden in 1670.</note>
**Syringa with flowers of a silvery hue.** <note>original: "Syringa flore quasi argenteo."</note>

**Mountain dwarf cherry with single blue fruit** of *Caspar Bauhin*. **Upright Woodbine III** of *Carolus Clusius*. <note>This is the Blue-berried Honeysuckle (*Lonicera caerulea*).</note>

**Alpine dwarf cherry with twin red fruit marked by two dots** of *Caspar Bauhin*. **The other Fly Honeysuckle** of *Rembert Dodoens*. <note>Likely *Lonicera alpigena*, the Alpine Honeysuckle.</note>

\* **Pyrenean dwarf cherry with olive-like leaves and twin red fruit similar to a gooseberry.**

### Storax with the leaf of a Quince of *Caspar Bauhin*.
**Storax tree** of *Jean Bauhin*. <note>The *Styrax officinalis*, a small tree from which a fragrant resin known as storax or benzoin was historically harvested for incense and medicine.</note>

### The Oxyacantha of Dioscorides, or the Sharp Thorn with a pear-like leaf of *Caspar Bauhin*.
**Firethorn** of the *Adversaria*. <insert>\* **Firethorn**</insert> <note>original: "Buisson ardent." The Latin *Oxyacantha* usually referred to Hawthorn, but the description "pear-leafed" and the French name *Buisson ardent* identify this specifically as *Pyracantha coccinea*. The "Adversaria" refers to the *Stirpium Adversaria Nova* (1570) by de l'Obel and Pena.</note>

See *Vidi maram* in the *Garden of Malabar* <note>original: "Hort. Mal."; referring to the "Hortus Malabaricus," a massive treatise on the plants of the Malabar Coast</note>; see also *Sebestena*.

**GOLDENROD** from **New York** with white flowers; with the leaf of the branched Canadian Daisy of Cornut. <note>Jacques-Philippe Cornut (1606–1651) wrote "Canadensium plantarum," the first book on North American flora.</note>
